summary: Describes the Zstandard (zstd) compression mechanism and registers a media type and content encoding for carrying zstd-compressed content in MIME. It is informational, as the word standard in the name does not make it an IETF standard. It was replaced by RFC 8878.

eli5.summary: Zstd squeezes files smaller, like vacuum-packing clothes. This gives it an official name so it can be sent in mail and web messages.

subtitle: A modern compression method for files, streams, and web content.

tldr.problem: Programs need efficient compression that balances speed and compression ratio for file storage, streaming, and web transport.
tldr.mechanism: Zstandard divides data into independent frames containing blocks of literals and match sequences, using Huffman coding for literals and Finite State Entropy (FSE) for match metadata.
tldr.outcome: Widely adopted for production use, especially at Facebook; superseded by RFC 8878.

today: RFC 8478 is Informational and defined the original Zstandard format. It has been obsoleted by RFC 8878, which updates the specification.

sections.title: What is Zstandard
sections.content:
Zstandard, or zstd, is a lossless data compression method similar to gzip, designed for modern use cases. Unlike its name, this RFC is informational only, not a standards-track specification. The RFC describes the compression format and registers two IANA entries: the application/zstd media type for identifying zstd-compressed content in mail and web messages, and a content encoding for HTTP.

Zstandard is notable for balancing compression ratio and speed. It operates independently of CPU type, operating system, file system, or character set, making it portable across diverse platforms.
sections.eli5: Zstd is a way to squish files down. It is designed to be both fast and good at squishing, so it works well everywhere from phones to big servers.

sections.title: Frames and Blocks
sections.content:
Zstandard data is organized as one or more independent frames, each with a magic number (4 bytes: 0xFD2FB528), a variable-size frame header (2-14 bytes), one or more data blocks, and an optional checksum. Multiple frames can be concatenated; decompressing them yields the concatenation of each frame's output.

Each frame is divided into one or more blocks, which depend on previous blocks for proper decoding but can be decompressed individually once earlier blocks are available. This enables streaming: the decompressor can output data as blocks arrive, without waiting for the entire frame. The frame header defines parameters like the decompressed content size, window size (memory buffer needed), dictionary ID, and whether a checksum is present.
sections.eli5: Compressed data is split into frames, like chapters in a book. Each frame has a header that says how big it is and what to expect. Inside are blocks of compressed content that can be unpacked one at a time.

sections.title: Literals and Sequences
sections.content:
Each block contains two parts: a literals section with uncompressed data bytes, and a sequences section with commands that reference those literals and copy from earlier decompressed data. A sequence is a pair of (literals length, offset, match length): copy N bytes from the literals section, then copy M bytes from N bytes back in the output.

Literals can be stored raw (uncompressed), as a run of identical bytes (RLE), or Huffman-compressed. Sequences are encoded compactly using Finite State Entropy (FSE) to represent the three symbol types—literals length, match length, and offset—interleaved in a single bitstream that decoders read backwards.
sections.eli5: Each block says: copy these raw bytes, then copy that part again from earlier. All the copying instructions are squished down with clever math so they take less space.

sections.title: Entropy Encoding
sections.content:
Zstandard uses two entropy codes. Huffman coding compresses literal bytes by assigning short bit patterns to common values and long patterns to rare ones. Huffman tables are described as weights (inversely related to bit length) and may be compressed themselves using FSE.

Finite State Entropy (FSE) is used for all other symbols: literals lengths, match lengths, and offsets. FSE is an entropy codec based on Asymmetric Numeral Systems. Each symbol type has a decoding table indexed by a state value; reading bits from the bitstream updates the state and yields the next symbol. Zstandard provides predefined FSE distributions for the three symbol types, or allows custom distributions in the compressed data.
sections.eli5: Zstd uses two tricks: Huffman coding for raw bytes (common bytes get short codes), and FSE for the copying instructions (which also get short codes). The decoder can either use preset codes or read custom ones from the file.

sections.title: Dictionaries
sections.content:
Zstandard supports optional dictionaries for improved compression of related data. A dictionary is provided out of band (not in the frame), and its ID is signaled in the frame header. A dictionary can be raw bytes or use a format that includes entropy tables and repeat offset hints.

While the RFC does not specify how dictionaries are obtained, it defines the format and notes that the low ID range (≤ 32767) and high range (≥ 2^31) are reserved for IANA-registered dictionaries. The content of a dictionary acts as prior decompressed data, allowing sequences to reference it as long as output has not exceeded the window size.
sections.eli5: For files that are all similar (like a folder of website logs), you can give the compressor a sample of common patterns. It remembers those patterns and can make compressed files smaller by reusing them.

sections.title: Security and Limitations
sections.content:
Compression can leak information about secret messages via analysis of compression ratios (the CRIME attack is a well-known example). Care must be taken not to compress data mixing a secret and untrusted content.

Decoders must validate frames carefully to prevent memory exhaustion attacks. An attacker may craft frames with unreasonable memory requirements (via large window sizes or frame content sizes). Fuzzing is recommended to harden decoder implementations. Arbitrary user metadata can be stored in skippable frames (magic 0x184D2A5?), which decoders ignore but can be used for watermarking or tracking.
sections.eli5: Be careful if you compress a secret mixed with data from the internet: the attacker might guess the secret by looking at the compressed size. Also, decoders should not trust huge memory sizes that attackers suggest.

fields.name: Frame Header
fields.desc: 2 to 14 bytes: descriptor, window size, dictionary ID, content size.

fields.name: Data Blocks
fields.desc: One or more: header (3 bytes) + content.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: Optional XXH64 checksum, if Content_Checksum_Flag is set.
